messages.author: 12cad5a425e186dd
messages.subject: Temporal trends in occupancy
parts:
We are thinking of looking for trends in occupancy through time with our camera trap data. We have several years of data for a given species, but the size of the occupancy matrix might be  different for each year. Putting all these in the same Occu data frame with a year covariate seems to make sense, but matrices from each year need to be the same size. I thought of just looking at the dimension of the biggest one and then adding NA rows and columns to the other ones to make them the same size.  Is there an easier way to do this?

Also, would colext would be more appropiate for this analysis?

Many thanks,

Jorge

messages.author: 20119867e986c754
messages.subject: Re: Temporal trends in occupancy
parts:
Did you keep the same sites, but missed some in some years, or did you
sample a different set of sites each year? If you did the latter,
then don't use colext() because you won't really be estimating the
true occupancy dynamics. I would think a dynamic model would be more
interesting because of the colonization and extinction parameters you
could estimate.

If you use occu() with year as a covariate, I guess you're first year
is the baseline, and each other year's beta is the change from the
first year. I suppose model selection between models that include the
year and one's that don't would be one way of inferring whether the
occupancy is changing over time.

You will need to add the NAs. Not sure what would be an easier way.

messages.author: 527e14923215b7e4
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Temporal trends in occupancy
parts:
Hi Jorge,

One problem with using single-season occupancy models to model multi-season data is that you are ignoring the serial correlation within sites among seasons. Put another way, the model would be assuming that you have a new random sample of sites each year, which you do not. This could lead to artificially small estimates of variance, but on the other hand, it is probably a reasonable place to begin.

The other option is to formally recognize the serial correlation using the MacKenzie et al. (2003) model, which can be implemented using colext. Trend is not a parameter per se, but you could compute it as a derived parameter. See

vignette("colext")

for more details. It is also possible to reformulate the MacKenzie et al. (2003) model so that you are modeling occupancy probability each year, instead of colonization and extinction. That might be another way of estimating trend, but that parameterization is not implemented in unmarked. I think it is in PRESENCE though. Regardless, I agree with Hardin that a multi-season model would probably be more appropriate here.

Richard
